metadata.title: Graphing Linear Relations and Modelling
metadata.vcaa_description: Graph linear relations on the Cartesian plane; use mathematical modelling to solve applied problems involving linear relations.
metadata.target_mastery: Plot linear relations on the Cartesian plane, determine gradient ($m$) and $y$-intercept ($c$) from $y = mx + c$, find the equation of a line from a table or two points, and model real-world linear relationships.
prerequisites: Plotting coordinates $(x, y)$ on the four-quadrant Cartesian plane

key_vocabulary.definition: A measure of the steepness and direction of a straight line, defined as $\text{gradient } m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$.
The $y$-intercept is the value of $y$ where a graph crosses the vertical $y$-axis (at $x = 0$). The $x$-intercept is the value of $x$ where a graph crosses the horizontal $x$-axis (at $y = 0$).
The equation of a non-vertical straight line written in the form $y = mx + c$, where $m$ is the gradient and $(0, c)$ is the $y$-intercept.

theory.title: Gradient ($m$) as Rise Over Run
theory.explanation: Between any two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ on a straight line, the ratio of the vertical change (rise) to the horizontal change (run) is constant. Moving from left to right: a line that slopes upwards has a positive gradient ($m > 0$), a line that slopes downwards has a negative gradient ($m < 0$), a horizontal line has zero gradient ($m = 0$), and a vertical line has an undefined gradient.
theory.callout_title: Read Graphs from Left to Right
theory.callout_rule: Always take run as positive (moving left to right). If the line goes up, rise is positive ($+$); if the line goes down, rise is negative ($-$).

theory.title: Gradient-Intercept Form ($y = mx + c$) and Axis Intercepts
theory.explanation: Every non-vertical straight line can be written as $y = mx + c$, where $m$ is the gradient (rate of change of $y$ per $1$-unit increase in $x$) and $c$ is the $y$-intercept (the value of $y$ when $x = 0$). To find the $x$-intercept of a line, substitute $y = 0$ and solve for $x$.
theory.formula_latex: y = mx + c: \quad y\text{-intercept at } (0, c), \quad x\text{-intercept at } \left(-\frac{c}{m}, 0\right)
theory.callout_title: Opposite Variable Equals Zero for Intercepts
theory.callout_rule: To find the $y$-intercept, set $x = 0$. To find the $x$-intercept, set $y = 0$.

theory.title: Linear Modelling in Practical Contexts
theory.explanation: Many real-world situations with a fixed starting value and a constant rate of change are modelled by a linear relation $y = mx + c$. In applied contexts, the $y$-intercept $c$ represents the initial value (when $x = 0$), and the gradient $m$ represents the constant rate of increase ($m > 0$) or decrease ($m < 0$) per unit of $x$.
theory.callout_title: Match Rate to $m$ and Initial Value to $c$
theory.callout_rule: When a tank starts with $500\text{ L}$ and drains at $20\text{ L/min}$, initial value $c = 500$ and rate $m = -20$, giving $V = -20t + 500$.

worked_examples.title: Finding the Gradient and Equation of a Line Through Two Points
worked_examples.problem: A straight line passes through the points $(0, -4)$ and $(3, 5)$. Find (a) the gradient $m$ of the line and (b) its equation in the form $y = mx + c$.

steps.thinking: Use the gradient formula $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ with $(x_1, y_1) = (0, -4)$ and $(x_2, y_2) = (3, 5)$.
Identify the $y$-intercept $c$ from the point $(0, -4)$, which gives $c = -4$, and substitute $m = 3$ and $c = -4$ into $y = mx + c$.

now_you_try.problem: A straight line passes through $(0, 7)$ and $(4, -1)$. Find (a) its gradient $m$ and (b) its equation in the form $y = mx + c$.

worked_examples.title: Finding the $x$- and $y$-Intercepts of a Linear Relation
worked_examples.problem: Find the coordinates of the $y$-intercept and the $x$-intercept of the line $3x + 4y = 24$.

steps.thinking: To find the $y$-intercept, substitute $x = 0$ into $3x + 4y = 24$ and solve for $y$.
To find the $x$-intercept, substitute $y = 0$ into $3x + 4y = 24$ and solve for $x$.

now_you_try.problem: Find the $y$-intercept and $x$-intercept of the line $2x - 5y = 20$.
now_you_try.hint: Set $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept ($-5y = 20$) and set $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept ($2x = 20$).

worked_examples.title: Linear Modelling of a Draining Water Tank
worked_examples.problem: A rural firefighting water tank near Horsham starts with $2400\text{ L}$ of water and is pumped out at a constant rate of $150\text{ L}$ per minute. (a) Write a linear rule for the volume $V\text{ (L)}$ remaining after $t$ minutes. (b) Find the volume remaining after $9$ minutes. (c) How many minutes does it take for the tank to empty completely?

steps.thinking: The initial volume at $t = 0$ is $c = 2400$ and the rate of change is $m = -150\text{ L/min}$. Write the rule $V = mt + c$ and evaluate at $t = 9$.
In part (c), the tank is empty when $V = 0$. Substitute $V = 0$ and solve for $t$.

now_you_try.problem: A hiker on the Overland Track is $36\text{ km}$ from Cradle Mountain Visitor Centre and walks towards it at a steady $4.5\text{ km/h}$. (a) Write a rule for her distance $D\text{ (km)}$ from the centre after $t$ hours. (b) How long until she reaches the centre ($D = 0$)?
now_you_try.hint: Initial distance $c = 36$, rate $m = -4.5$. Set $D = 0$ for part (b).

common_misconceptions.title: Inverting Gradient as Run Over Rise
common_misconceptions.misconception: Calculating gradient as run over rise ($\frac{x_2 - x_1}{y_2 - y_1}$) instead of rise over run ($\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$).
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Gradient measures vertical change per unit of horizontal change, so the difference in $y$-coordinates ($\text{rise}$) is always in the numerator and the difference in $x$-coordinates ($\text{run}$) is always in the denominator.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: As $x$ increases by $2$ (from $1$ to $3$), $y$ increases by $6$ (from $2$ to $8$), which is $3$ units of rise for every $1$ unit of run.

common_misconceptions.title: Confusing Term Order with $m$ and $c$ in $y = c + mx$
common_misconceptions.misconception: Assuming the first number written on the RHS of a linear equation is always the gradient $m$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: The gradient $m$ is always the coefficient of $x$, and the $y$-intercept $c$ is the constant term, regardless of the order in which the terms are written.
common_misconceptions.incorrect_working: $$\text{In } y = 12 - 5x, \text{ gradient } m = 12 \text{ and } y\text{-intercept } c = -5 \quad \text{(Incorrect)}$$

fluency_and_understanding.question: State the gradient $m$ and the $y$-intercept $c$ of the line $y = 15 - 4x$.
step_by_step_solution: Rewrite $y = 15 - 4x$ in gradient-intercept form $y = mx + c$: $y = -4x + 15$.
Read off the coefficient of $x$ as $m = -4$ and the constant term as $c = 15$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Find the gradient of the straight line passing through the points $(-2, 5)$ and $(4, 23)$.
Find the gradient and the equation of the line passing through $(0, 9)$ and $(5, -6)$.
step_by_step_solution: Calculate the gradient: $m = \frac{-6 - 9}{5 - 0} = \frac{-15}{5} = -3$.
Since the line passes through $(0, 9)$, the $y$-intercept is $c = 9$, giving $y = -3x + 9$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Find the $y$-intercept and the $x$-intercept of the line $y = 4x - 20$.
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $x = 0$: $y = 4(0) - 20 = -20$, so the $y$-intercept is $(0, -20)$.
Substitute $y = 0$: $0 = 4x - 20 \implies 4x = 20 \implies x = 5$, so the $x$-intercept is $(5, 0)$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A table of values for a linear relation shows $(x, y)$ pairs: $(1, 11), (2, 15), (3, 19), (4, 23)$. Find the linear rule in the form $y = mx + c$.
step_by_step_solution: As $x$ increases by $1$, $y$ increases by $4$, so the gradient is $m = 4$.
Substitute $(1, 11)$ into $y = 4x + c$: $11 = 4(1) + c \implies c = 7$. Thus $y = 4x + 7$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Find the equation of the straight line passing through the two points $(2, 1)$ and $(6, 13)$ in the form $y = mx + c$.
step_by_step_solution: Calculate the gradient: $m = \frac{13 - 1}{6 - 2} = \frac{12}{4} = 3$.
Substitute $m = 3$ and the point $(2, 1)$ into $y = mx + c$: $1 = 3(2) + c \implies c = -5$, giving $y = 3x - 5$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A Melbourne Myki card holds a balance of $\$50$ at the start of the month. Each daily full-fare Zone 1+2 commute deducts $\$10.60$ from the balance. (a) Write a linear rule for the balance $B\text{ (\$)}$ after $d$ days of travel. (b) What is the balance after $4$ days of travel?
step_by_step_solution: Initial balance is $c = 50$ and daily change is $m = -10.6$, so $B = -10.6d + 50$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: At Mount Buller, the depth of snow $S\text{ (cm)}$ at the base station starts at $65\text{ cm}$ at midnight and increases during a blizzard at a constant rate of $3.5\text{ cm}$ per hour for $t$ hours. (a) Write a rule for $S$ in terms of $t$. (b) After how many hours does the snow depth reach $93\text{ cm}$?
step_by_step_solution: With initial depth $c = 65$ and rate $m = 3.5$, the linear rule is $S = 3.5t + 65$.
Substitute $S = 93$: $93 = 3.5t + 65 \implies 3.5t = 28 \implies t = \frac{28}{3.5} = 8\text{ hours}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A straight line has $x$-intercept $(6, 0)$ and $y$-intercept $(0, 8)$. Calculate the area of the right-angled triangle enclosed by this line, the $x$-axis, and the $y$-axis.
step_by_step_solution: The line intersects the positive $x$-axis at $6$ (base $= 6$ units) and the positive $y$-axis at $8$ (perpendicular height $= 8$ units).
Calculate the area of the right-angled triangle: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24\text{ square units}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Determine algebraically whether the point $(12, -29)$ lies on the straight line $y = -3x + 7$. Justify your conclusion.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Yes, $(12, -29)$ lies on the line because substituting $x = 12$ gives $y = -29$
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $x = 12$ into the right-hand side of $y = -3x + 7$: $y = -3(12) + 7 = -36 + 7 = -29$.
Since the calculated $y$-value ($-29$) matches the $y$-coordinate of the point $(12, -29)$, the point lies on the line.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Explain why a vertical line (such as $x = 4$) has an undefined gradient, whereas a horizontal line (such as $y = 4$) has a gradient of $0$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Horizontal line has $\text{rise} = 0$ ($m = \frac{0}{\text{run}} = 0$); vertical line has $\text{run} = 0$ ($m = \frac{\text{rise}}{0}$, which is undefined)
step_by_step_solution: On a horizontal line $y = 4$, any two points have the same $y$-coordinate, so $\text{rise} = 0$ and $m = \frac{0}{\text{run}} = 0$.
On a vertical line $x = 4$, any two points have the same $x$-coordinate, so $\text{run} = 0$. Because division by zero is undefined, $m = \frac{\text{rise}}{0}$ is undefined.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Three points $A(1, 3)$, $B(4, 15)$, and $C(7, k)$ are collinear (they lie on the same straight line). Use gradients to find the value of $k$.
step_by_step_solution: Find the gradient of segment $AB$: $m_{AB} = \frac{15 - 3}{4 - 1} = \frac{12}{3} = 4$.
Since $A, B, C$ are collinear, the gradient of $BC$ must also equal $4$: $\frac{k - 15}{7 - 4} = 4 \implies \frac{k - 15}{3} = 4 \implies k - 15 = 12 \implies k = 27$.
